subject: Business Models
title: Value-Based Pricing
description: A quick, practical guide to Value-Based Pricing.

hook.text: A cancer drug costs $2 to make and sells for $100,000. The price reflects what it's worth, not what it costs.

buildup.text: Value-based pricing sets the price based on benefits delivered, not production expenses.

discovery.text: Software is the ultimate example: near-zero marginal cost, priced entirely on perceived value.

twist.text: This only works when buyers can perceive the value. If they can't tell the difference, they buy cheap.

climax.text: Luxury brands, consulting firms, and tech companies all thrive on value-based pricing.

punchline.text: Price what it's worth, not what it costs. That's the margin.

quiz.question: What determines the price in value-based pricing?

details.summary: Value-based pricing sets prices according to the customer's perceived value of the product rather than production costs or competitor prices. A tool that saves a company one million dollars annually can justify a hundred thousand dollar price tag regardless of its development cost.
details.whyItMatters: Value-based pricing captures a share of the value created for customers rather than settling for cost-plus margins. Companies that master it consistently achieve higher margins and stronger competitive positions than cost-based competitors.
takeaways: Price is set based on customer value received, not production cost
Requires deep understanding of how customers measure and receive value
Enables significantly higher margins than cost-plus or competitive pricing

faq.question: How do you determine the right price in value-based pricing?
faq.answer: Quantify the specific value your product creates for customers through time savings, revenue increases, or cost reductions. Then price at a fraction of that value, typically 10-20%. If your tool saves a customer $500,000 annually, pricing at $50,000 to $100,000 is justified.

faq.question: Why is value-based pricing difficult to implement in practice?
faq.answer: It requires deep customer research to understand how each segment perceives value. Different customers derive different value from the same product. Sales teams must communicate value clearly. Customers accustomed to cost-based pricing may resist premium pricing.
